newsitem.title: GERMANY: Archive shows Germany planned WWII from 1925.
newsitem.headline: Archive shows Germany planned WWII from 1925.

text.p: Recently discovered records show Germany began planning for World War Two as early as 1925, 10 years before Adolf Hitler trampled on the Versailles Treaty and began openly rearming, a leading weekly said on Thursday.

Die Zeit said secret German plans found in the National Archives in Washington called for the limited 100,000-strong force allowed after World War One to expand up to the 2.8 million men Hitler had when he invaded Poland in 1939.

Even the structure of the Nazi forces -- eight complete armies, 102 divisions and 252 generals -- matched the plan commissioned by Reichswehr General Hans von Seeckt while Hitler was still a small-time rabble-rouser in Munich, it said.
"This document was lying unnoticed in the Pentagon for many years," Die Zeit wrote in a special report on the find by an amateur Hamburg historian Carl Dirks, a wartime tank officer.

"If the prosecutors at the Nuremberg war crimes trial had known about it, the German general staff would probably not have been acquitted but would have been indicted for conspiring against the peace."

The discovery of the long-lost binder full of armaments plans dealt another blow to the post-war myth of a "clean" and professional Wehrmacht army, originally known as Reichswehr, that was misused by Hitler.

A photo exhibition that opened amid protests from neo-Nazis and left-wingers in Munich in late February has proven the Wehrmacht also took part in Holocaust killings alongside the SS thugs blamed for massacres of civilians on the eastern front.
According to Die Zeit Dirks, who after the war helped Scotland Yard police translate Nazi documents seized by British troops, found the rearmament plan while researching a book.

The plan was the "key document" that proved historians' long-held suspicions that the military elite planned revenge for Germany's World War One defeat even before Hitler came to power in 1933 and ordered rearmament, Die Zeit said.

A 1960 note about the plan by Walter Behschnitt, one of the officers who drew it up, called the preparations "the most secret of secrets" and said participants had to use false names and were sworn to secrecy, Die Zeit said.
The plan focused on preparing the armed forces for war rather than determining the strategy Germany should use to take revenge for Versailles and regain its powerful role in Europe.
Its financial demands were so great that the Reichswehr, as the armed forces were called between 1919 and 1935, had a secret budget from the late 1920s to top up its normal funding.
Die Zeit said the plan was a reaction to the French and Belgian occupation of the Ruhr industrial belt in 1923 and aimed to prepare Germany for the time it could strike back.
It said the army had be ready to fight from 1935, when France's defences would start to weaken because of a fall in birthrates dating back to the first war.

According to Die Zeit, Hitler completely adopted the generals' secret plan after coming to power in 1933, including its call for German society to be indirectly militarised through mass sports programmes in preparation for a total war.
Hitler broke the Versailles Treaty in 1935, gave the Reichswehr the new name Wehrmacht and set out on the open rearmament programme that led to war four years later.
"The generals...never lost sight of their goal of a large army," Die Zeit wrote. "The framework was set up in 1925 and only had to be filled out."
